outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: This section will provide a concise summary of the entire survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) security from 2023 to 2026. It will briefly outline the shift from identifying baseline vulnerabilities to the current co-evolutionary arms race between sophisticated offensive weaponization and dynamic defensive interventions. The abstract will summarize the four core threat vectors analyzed: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations. It will also emphasize the survey's contribution in systematizing testing methodologies and cross-cutting defenses, providing a holistic view of the LLM security landscape and outlining critical open challenges for future research.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: The introduction will establish the motivation for the survey, contextualizing the explosive deployment of LLMs and MLLMs in high-stakes domains and the corresponding surge in security vulnerabilities. It will define the scope of the paper, focusing on the critical temporal evolution from 2023 to 2026, a period marked by a transition from static, rule-based defenses to dynamic, automated adversarial arms races. The section will outline the survey's core contributions: a comprehensive taxonomy of threats spanning the model lifecycle (training-time poisoning to inference-time prompt injection and hallucinations), a critical analysis of state-of-the-art testing methodologies, and a synthesis of cross-cutting defense strategies. It will explicitly map the structure of the paper, guiding the reader through the subsequent sections on background, specific threat vectors, evaluation frameworks, and future directions.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section will establish the foundational concepts and terminology required to understand the LLM security landscape. It will provide a brief overview of modern LLM and MLLM architectures, including alignment techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and retrieval mechanisms. Crucially, it will define a comprehensive threat model, categorizing adversaries based on their capabilities (black-box vs. white-box) and their access points across the model lifecycle (training, alignment, and inference phases). The section will also introduce the conceptual shift from unimodal text-based vulnerabilities to complex, multimodal, and agentic attack vectors, setting the stage for the detailed threat analyses in the subsequent sections.

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section will analyze the evolution of Data and Model Poisoning attacks from 2024 to 2025. It will detail the shift from unimodal text-based vulnerabilities to highly complex, multimodal, and embodied AI attack vectors. The discussion will begin with foundational 2024 studies, referencing works like [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm], which benchmarked generative backdoors in open-source models such as LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J. It will highlight how traditional defenses proved inadequate against these generative threats. The section will then explore the late 2024/early 2025 turning point, focusing on the exploitation of alignment and retrieval mechanisms, particularly the vulnerabilities discovered within the RLHF pipeline, which was previously considered a robust safety alignment tool. The analysis will emphasize how attackers are now targeting the complex system architectures that make modern AI functional.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: Focusing on the 2024-2026 timeframe, this section will examine the rapid evolution of adversarial attacks and defenses in LLMs and MLLMs. It will begin by discussing the identification of baseline vulnerabilities in high-stakes, specialized domains. A key focus will be the alarming susceptibility of models deployed in critical sectors like healthcare, specifically referencing [Yang_2024_Adversarial] and the manipulation of sensitive datasets like MIMIC-III. The narrative will then transition to the sophisticated, multi-faceted arms race characterized by advanced offensive weaponization. It will contrast early 'patchwork' defensive wrappers with more surgical interventions, highlighting early successes like the contrastive prompt tuning introduced by [Wang_2024_Advqdet], which achieved up to 99% detection rates against query-based black-box attacks. The section will emphasize the shift toward integrated, architectural defenses.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section will cover the transformative evolution of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks between 2025 and 2026. It will document the definitive shift from static, rule-based defenses to a highly dynamic, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial arms race. The text will detail how attackers successfully automated the discovery of adversarial prompts using adaptive optimization techniques. Specific attention will be given to the application of modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, referencing the pivotal works of [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. The section will highlight the alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) of 50% to 71% achieved against state-of-the-art LLM agents. Finally, it will explore the bifurcation of this trend into the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency and the development of dynamic, ensemble-based attack systems.

outline.title: Output Integrity and Reliability: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: This section will trace the sophisticated evolution of research on LLM hallucinations and factual consistency from 2023 to 2026. It will describe the fundamental shift from basic, computationally expensive detection mechanisms to highly optimized, mechanistically informed frameworks. The discussion will start with the 2023 baseline, where LLMs were leveraged as evaluators to police themselves. A landmark development to be highlighted is ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM], which demonstrated that LLM-based polling and Chain-of-Thought prompting could drastically reduce inference costs (using only a quarter of contemporary competitors' costs) while outperforming them. The section will then explore the conceptual maturation that occurred in 2024, where the field moved beyond treating all non-factual generations as binary errors, adopting more nuanced, context-aware, and mechanistically grounded approaches to factual consistency.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section will provide a holistic overview of defense mechanisms that span across the various threat categories. It will synthesize the transition from early 'patchwork' and external stateful detection wrappers to deeply integrated, architectural defenses. The discussion will cover prompt-level manipulations, such as the contrastive prompt tuning utilized for black-box attack detection [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. It will also address the development of dynamic, ensemble-based defensive systems designed to counter automated optimization attacks (like GCG and MCTS fuzzing). Furthermore, the section will explore mitigation strategies for training-time vulnerabilities, including robust RLHF pipelines and alignment techniques designed to resist generative backdoors and multimodal poisoning. The focus will be on how defenses are co-evolving with the increasingly automated and sophisticated offensive techniques.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This MANDATORY dedicated section will critically analyze the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks used across all covered threat categories. It will synthesize how the community measures security and reliability. Key datasets discussed will include high-stakes domain data like MIMIC-III (used in adversarial healthcare attacks [Yang_2024_Adversarial]). The section will evaluate standard metrics, contrasting the 99% detection rates in early query-based defenses [Wang_2024_Advqdet] with the alarming 50-71% Attack Success Rates (ASR) seen in automated jailbreaks [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM]. It will also deeply examine the 'LLM-as-a-judge' paradigm, evaluating tools like ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM] for their computational efficiency in hallucination detection. Furthermore, it will address the benchmarking of generative backdoors in models like LLaMA-2 and Mistral [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking], highlighting the urgent need for standardized, dynamic evaluation frameworks that can keep pace with automated adversarial optimization.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section will critically synthesize the current state of LLM security, identifying major gaps, limitations, and open challenges. It will discuss the fundamental asymmetry between attackers, who leverage highly automated, computationally efficient optimization techniques (e.g., genetic algorithms, MCTS), and defenders, who often rely on reactive, computationally expensive guardrails. The discussion will highlight the unresolved vulnerabilities in multimodal and embodied AI systems, where the attack surface expands significantly beyond text. It will also address the limitations of current alignment mechanisms (like RLHF) against sophisticated poisoning. Finally, it will propose future research directions, emphasizing the need for provable security guarantees, mechanistically interpretable models, and proactive, dynamic defense frameworks capable of anticipating co-evolutionary threats.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will provide a final synthesis of the survey's findings, reiterating the rapid maturation of the LLM security landscape from 2023 to 2026. It will summarize the critical shift from isolated, unimodal vulnerabilities to complex, automated, and multimodal adversarial ecosystems. The section will offer practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments, emphasizing the necessity of moving beyond static guardrails toward integrated, dynamic, and mechanistically informed security postures. It will close with a forward-looking statement on the critical importance of secure AI alignment for the future of foundation models.
